extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; citizens and policymakers considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A set of argumentative expositions defending specific provisions of the proposed U.S. Constitution (ratification rules, prohibitions on state powers, federal powers such as the Necessary and Proper clause and Supremacy clause), aimed at persuading citizens to ratify. The text explains the meaning, necessity, and likely consequences of each constitutional provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification by nine States sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ratification of the conventions of nine States shall be sufficient for the establishment of this Constitution between the States, ratifying the same."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that express authority of the people (conventions) gives validity; unanimous ratification would subject whole to caprice or corruption of a single State. Justifies using conventions rather than unanimous consent to avoid paralysis and safeguard the essential interests of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supersession of the Confederation without unanimous consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Confederation may be superseded without unanimous consent when absolute necessity, self-preservation, or repeated infractions by parties justify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues by appeal to the 'great principle of self-preservation' and analogies from treaty law: where one party breaches mutual conditions, others may treat the compact as violated and withdraw. Also notes many State ratifications under the Confederation were only legislative, reducing the Confederation's claim to immutable validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of ratifying and non-ratifying States
rubrics_metrics.description: Although no political relation can subsist between assenting and dissenting States, moral relations, claims of justice, and rights of humanity remain and must be respected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates moderation and prudence on both sides, expecting moral obligations and mutual respect to endure, and hopes for reconciliation through common interest and remembrance of past bonds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not enter into treaties, alliances, or confederations
rubrics_metrics.description: "No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copied from existing articles of Union — ensures uniformity in foreign relations and prevents individual States from compromising national responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not grant letters of marque and reprisal except under federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: "grant letters of marque and reprisal;" (must be obtained from the government of the United States during war or prior to its declaration)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends existing limitation so such licenses are uniformly issued by the federal government, ensuring uniformity in foreign affairs and national responsibility for maritime conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not coin money
rubrics_metrics.description: "coin money;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing coinage from States avoids multiple mints, diversified weights and forms, and expensive reminting; centralizes coinage to prevent impediments to interstate commerce and confusion in currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not emit bills of credit (issue paper money)
rubrics_metrics.description: "emit bills of credit;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper money issuance by States has produced 'pestilent effects' — destroyed confidence, harmed industry and morals, and destabilized republican government. The prohibition aims to prevent these public harms and restore fiscal stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction: States may not make anything but gold and silver a legal tender
rubrics_metrics.description: "make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On same principle as prohibiting paper currency; prevents retrospective alterations in value that injure citizens and hinder interstate and foreign confidence and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts are forbidden to States
rubrics_metrics.description: "pass any bill of attainder, ex post facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures contravene first principles of social compact and sound legislation; the prohibition provides an added constitutional safeguard for personal security and private rights, and prevents speculations and legislative abuses that harm industry and the less-informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not grant titles of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: "or grant any title of nobility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carried over from the Articles of Confederation; intended to prevent aristocratic distinctions incompatible with republican principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on state imposts/duties on imports and exports without Congress's consent
rubrics_metrics.description: "No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and the net produce ... shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secures uniform regulation of trade and reserves net revenue to the United States; balances reasonable state discretion for inspection with federal oversight to prevent abuse and inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not lay duties on tonnage without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: "No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of restraints to ensure uniform maritime and commercial policy and to prevent individual States from disrupting national commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not keep troops or ships of war in time of peace without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: "keep troops or ships of war in time of peace,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents individual States from maintaining standing forces that could disturb national security and interstate harmony; aligns military posture under federal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition: States shall not enter agreements or compacts with other States or foreign powers without Congress's consent
rubrics_metrics.description: "enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids conflicting foreign or inter-state obligations that could undermine national unity and consistency in external affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction: States shall not engage in war unless actually invaded or in imminent danger
rubrics_metrics.description: "or engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents individual States from initiating hostilities that would embroil the Union; allows only urgent self-defense absent federal authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper Clause (power to make laws needed to execute federal powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: "power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defended as essential: without its substance the Constitution would be a 'dead letter.' Alternatives (strictly express enumeration, negative enumeration, silence) are critiqued; the clause allows means appropriate to accomplish constitutional ends. Remedies for any federal overreach include executive/judicial check and ultimate accountability to the people via elections; States are expected to be vigilant defenders of their rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy against misconstruction of federal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress misconstrues this power and exercises unwarranted authority, the check lies with the executive and judiciary departments and ultimately with the people who can elect new representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains institutional checks and popular remedy; asserts states will be especially alert to federal usurpations because federal acts invade state rights, thereby mobilizing local influence against unconstitutional federal acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy Clause: Constitution and federal laws are supreme law of the land
rubrics_metrics.description: "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties ... shall be the supreme law of the land, and the judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues necessity: without supremacy, federal powers would be annulled wherever state constitutions reserved sovereignty. Differing state constitutions could make national laws effective in some states and void in others, creating chaos and inversion of proper federal/part relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath to support the Constitution for various officers
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Senators and Representatives, and the members of the several State legislatures, and all executive and judicial officers, both of the United States and the several States, shall be bound by oath or affirmation to support this Constitution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justified as necessary to bind State magistracy (who have essential agency in giving effect to the federal Constitution) to federal obligations. Distinction drawn that federal officers need not be bound to state constitutions because federal officers will not administer state constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal powers are few and defined; State powers numerous and indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers delegated to the federal government are 'few and defined', principally external (war, peace, negotiation, foreign commerce); those remaining to the States are 'numerous and indefinite', covering internal affairs affecting lives, liberties, properties, and internal order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue federal government will not overwhelm state governments: the federal role is concentrated and often situational (war/danger), while states retain broad authority over daily civil life and will enjoy advantages in numbers, local influence, and frequency of peaceful interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of influence between State and Federal governments
rubrics_metrics.description: State governments will likely have advantages in personal influence, number of officers, and immediate dependence of elections, making them less likely to be absorbed by federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains mechanisms: state control over presidential and senatorial selection, larger number of local officers, greater presence across districts, and the different spheres of operation (peace vs war) all favor state influence and resist federal consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of constitutional change as invigoration not enlargement
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Constitution changes the Union less by adding new powers than by making original powers of the Union more effectually administered; e.g., regulation of commerce is new but most other principal powers existed under the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframes objections: taxation and other powers are not substantially increased in kind, only in the mode of administration; argues this does not threaten state existence but remedies inefficacy under the Confederation.
